fragments.text: Good morning, and I'm very pleased to be here with you at the 6th AI for IAA Conference, Artificial Intelligence for Information Accessibility Conference 2025. This is a conference that put people at the center of the conversation on artificial intelligence. From healthcare to do curriculum to the workplace, AI is increasingly becoming part of our everyday lives. But this growing presence also comes with responsibility. Today's focus is not just on what AI can do, but you know how it does it and for whom. It's more important now than ever to make this system understandable, trustworthy and inclusive. And today's discussion will help us explore AI, not just as a technical tool, but as something that is really affecting the way our societies and our economies work,

which reflect the choices, values and power structures behind it. Artificial Intelligence has been rapidly transforming the way we work, the way we live, the way we interact with people, and it's also growing in an economic sense. The market for artificial intelligence is estimated to have been growing beyond $244 billion US dollars in 2025. And according to some UN trade and development data, you know, they project that the global AI market will store from $189 billion in 2023 to $4.83 trillion by 2033. So basically a 25 fold increase in just a decade. These are estimates, so we don't know exactly how the trajectory will be, but nevertheless, this gives us an idea about the potential.

And this potential is not just concentrated in Europe or North America, but for instance, in Latin America and the Caribbean, the region hosting this conference, 47% of companies in the region will have implemented AI in their processes with another 40% exploring its use in 2023. And this is some data coming from an IBM report. In Asia, in Southeast Asia, the region when I'm based, AI is expected to provide between 10 and 18% GDP uplift across the region by 2030, which is equivalent to nearly one trillion US dollars to the local economy. It's very important to recognize AI global relevance. And this is something that the UN has been doing very well. Indeed, the global digital compact led by the UN was adopted during the latest 2024

UN General Assembly alongside the pact for the future. And this is a global framework to guide cooperation on digital technology and AI governance while at the same time addressing persistent digital divides. So I've just mentioned that there is a lot of opportunity, but the stark reality is that there are many inequalities across income, gender, geography. And this is something that is not only alarming, but also a trend that unfortunately continues to accelerate. For example, the latest global gender gap indexed for the World Economic Forum shows that no country has achieved full gender parity and the progress has been very slow. So it will take 123 years for a full global parity to be achieved according to their estimates.

So we can see that there's still a very long way to go. So AI can help. Probably there are some studies telling us that it can help accelerating almost 80% of the actions or activities related to the sustainable development goals. For example, AI can be very helpful in data driven analysis, predictive modelling, to help improving decision-making, increasing transparency, streamlining operations, and answering research management. And also finding personalized solutions, such as, for instance, feeding up a delivery in the development work. It can also be an opportunity for certain vulnerable groups by opening access, for instance, to financial services, which were once out of service, as it helps bypass traditional administrative and geographical barriers. So it can become very important when, you know, 1.4 billion adults were wild,

still lack access to basic financial services. So this brings me to some of the examples of the work we are currently undertaking at area, and I'm personally involved in it, related to these issues. So we have recently worked with the government of Korea, actually a body called Asam SME a co-innovation center, which is connected to the Korean Ministry for Startups and SMEs, to produce a study report on deep tech startups for sustainable development. And we also have recently published a white paper on the innovation ecosystem in Southeast Asia. And there, we could identify detailed examples of how startups, and especially tech-based startups, are really achieving solutions for the green transformation to bridging the gender gap, you know, or promoting cleaner oceans,

health tech, fintech, and much more. You will find all of these information in the reports that encourage to read and look for. And we're also very pleased to work in a collaborative way, including with many UN agencies. For example, an initiative I'm very proud of and to collaborate with is the UN Trade and Development Initiative called Itrade for Women, which is an activity aiming to empower women entrepreneurs in emerging markets by harnessing the transformative power of digital technologies to drive inclusive growth and innovation. And it's both a capacity-building initiative, but also a platform for women-led businesses to connect, exchange knowledge, and grow. And we really want to make sure that women-led businesses, especially those businesses connected

to the SDGs, and based on technology, including AI, from Southeast Asia, from Asia to large, are really increasingly connected to this initiative. And this is why we organized with ANGTA, a series of master classes, one in Jakarta, one in Delhi, and soon one in Manila, precisely to increase participation from Southeast Asia. Another project where we are really trying to understand the linkages between artificial intelligence and the SDGs is an activity that we are jointly undertaking with the ASAN Institute for Peace and Reconciliation, ASAN IPR. We have a joint project to try to understand the connection between the Women Peace and Security Agenda and the Women in the Digital Economy Agenda. And there we are really looking at how

digital technologies can be an enabler for peaceful economic development, or in other cases instead can be caused for a conflict or gender-based technology-faceted violence, so something that is very negative. We really want to look at the technology in a neutral way, Jan, and understand how can you maximize the good and minimize the bad. And another area where we have been very active is the investigation of the relationship between digital technology, including AI and disability. For instance, we have recently published a report with Title Technology and Disability Trans and Opportunity in the Digital Economy in ASAN, where we try to understand what are the current trends. And this is very important because persons with disability

they represent 15% of the world population, roughly 690 million people in ASAN the Pacific. So it's really a big number so we cannot forget about them. And what we saw in our report is that AI power solutions are emerging to actually make workplaces more inclusive, so to make sure that persons with different kind of disability, visible and invisible disability, thanks to technology them good can actually be more productive and better participate in societies and economies. So we looked at, for instance, assistive technology from glasses, wheelchairs, hearing aids, to eye tracking software that can solve and also transform solve problems and transform lives of persons with disability. And in these projects, we also looked a little bit at how digital literacy

remain a key barrier to access digital jobs, making demand-led training and upskilling programs a critical issue, I mean a critical resource, especially for persons with disability in Asia, but also worldwide. So to conclude AI holds great potential for inclusive development but we need to make sure that we are doing it right. And we also develop frameworks and guidelines and rules that are really steering systems in the right direction. So this is a concerting effort requiring responsible leadership, involving many different stakeholders, policymakers, technologists, companies, the private sector, SMEs, I mean a very very different community of stakeholders, creators, innovators, users. And global cooperation really needs to be at the forefront. These are problems or even opportunities that it's very difficult to rip, to benefit from

if we want to work in isolated AI ecosystems. When we combine resources, share knowledge and expand access to technology, we can really empower more people to take the lead in creating progress. So while AI developments hold many exciting possibilities, one thing remains clear, its future must be people centered, transparent, fair, inclusive and really rooted in shared global values, such as the sustainable development goals. Thank you very much.
